newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed sees steady, boring '97 U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed sees steady, boring '97 U.S. economy.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago said on Tuesday the U.S. economy is likely to post an average, boring performance in 1997.
"In 1997, forecasters are expecting a fairly boring year," Chicago Fed senior economists William Strauss and Robert Schnorbus said in a paper about the U.S. economic outlook.

"But boring is not necessarily bad, considering that not a single forecaster is expecting a recession over the next five quarters," the economists also said in their joint report compiling the results of a symposium the Chicago Fed held in December.
About 50 private and government economists took part in the conference.

The economists' consensus forecast called for the Gross Domestic Product to expand by 2.2 percent in 1997, the Consumer Price Index to rise by 2.8 percent, and the unemployment rate to average 5.5 percent.

"There was very widespread support for continued slow growth. The range of limits of the (GDP) forecasts were 1.4 percent and 2.6 percent," the Chicago Fed economists said in the conference's summary the bank made public on Tuesday.
"This slow economic growth will be good news for inflation watchers as price pressures on the economy are not expected to be strong," the economists added.

The conference, entitled "Building a House for the 21st Century," also noted the surprising strength of the U.S. housing sector in 1996 and forecast "the housing market should continue to do well in 1997."
